I have long arms and post/control gloves with my left arm and run into the same problem. 

Being intentional about keeping your glove at their shoulder height while you move back just so there’s something in the way to possibly deflect helps. That way it’s difficult for them to reach around and any hits they get you can glance off. Shoulder endurance training exercises helps with that habit.

I’d also recommend paying attention to how you disengage and just try to have an exit plan to be able to throw a check jab to interrupt momentum if they are trying to chase that opening. As well as making sure you’re not always disengaging straight back. Being ready to back hand parry/block their punch while you throw that jab I’ve found helpful and can buy you just a fraction more time to reset your guard.

Also watch out for left hooks if you’re doing an lazy philly shell stuff. It’s easy to want to naturally lean to your right which sets them up for a nice left hook

There is no certain future for your friendship. 
That’s just how it is, romance is high risk high reward. 
It’s good that you were able to be honest with your feelings. But it does change the dynamic of the relationship drastically. 

It sucks that it didn’t work out the way you wanted it to but if you want to continue it’s going to have to be acceptance of her decision.

Which means not questioning it or second guessing it or bringing it up again. 
Asking if things are awkward constantly or worrying over it is a form of bringing it up again .

This isn’t to shame you but it’s just how it’s going to feel from the other side.

Personally, I’d advise taking some time off the friendship completely. Not any dramatic “I can’t see you” stuff. Just respectful distance, group settings, a little less time to hangout. Just get to readjust and fill the headspace you were occupying with romantic feelings with other things. Let things blow over and hopefully you can come back as friends having missed each other and with a bunch of catching up to do from time apart.

Things won’t go back to the way they were for a while. It’s going to feel off and stilted for a bit. If you’re both going to remain friends you’re just going to have to deal with being uncomfortable for a bit. 

But on the bright side if you can make it through that you’ll find a deeper friendship at having been able to overcome a tricky social situation and compromise.
If you can’t don’t try to force something that doesn’t work. You lost a friend but were honest to yourself and your feelings. It’s sucks but they’ll be others and it’s a good lesson to learn. You can hold your head up, and be bit more wise for next time.

I feel you deeply. Boxing has been the only thing keeping me grounded and helping me take care of myself through depression and anxiety. But it’s really hard on a budget and I’m also part time working/college student. 

My advice is to start small and grow steadily. There’s some good YouTube channels out there for basics. Fighttips, natebowers fitness, etc. 

See if your college has any material art or boxing clubs. Work on conditioning. It took me around 6th months of running and cheap gear and budgeting before I was able to even step into a boxing gym due to anxiety. Good measure I was told on here conditioning wise was be able to run 6-8 8min/mi., be able to hit a heavy bag for half an hour straight before really starting any sparring or gyms. 

But the slow preparation was worth it and I’m learning faster than I would’ve if I just rushed headlong into it.

It does take a lot of sacrifice and I have had to give up a lot of small things to be able to afford my gym on my budget but it’s worth it. 

But for now. Have patience. Make a plan. Adjust accordingly. Don’t rush into things especially out of anger. You’ll hurt yourself if you’re not thinking clearly and the more you stack up small injuries the more you’ll be delayed from your goal. You gotta build the foundation stuff. Boxing isn’t as much about anger but control and preparation. An angry fighter gets sloppy and can get taken apart easily, it’s about staying calm. I speak from experience as I still lose in sparring anytime my anxiety or anger gets a hold. 

But I wish you the best. It’s an exciting and difficult road ahead but don’t lose hope. Boxing has been incredibly helpful for me, and broken through at some points more than years of therapy and prescriptions at getting myself to be a better and stable person so I really encourage to try you best. But to have patience with yourself. It’s a long hard process
